subject: Climate & Environment
title: Biodiversity in the Canopy
description: A micro-lesson that makes Biodiversity in the Canopy usable.

hook.text: Scientists once fogged a single tree in Panama with insecticide. 1,200 beetle species fell out.

buildup.text: The forest canopy is a world unto itself — a maze of branches, vines, and epiphytes.

discovery.text: Over half of all land species live in forests, and most of them live in the canopy.

twist.text: Many canopy species have never been studied. We lose them before knowing they exist.

climax.text: A single hectare of tropical forest can hold more tree species than all of North America.

punchline.text: The treetops hold species we haven't even named yet.

quiz.question: Where do most land species live?

details.summary: Tropical forest canopies are among the most species-rich habitats on Earth, housing an estimated 40 to 60 percent of all terrestrial species. Epiphytes, insects, birds, and arboreal mammals form complex communities that are lost entirely when the canopy is removed.
details.whyItMatters: Canopy life is poorly studied yet immensely diverse. When forests are cleared, canopy species disappear long before they are ever cataloged.
takeaways: A single canopy tree may host thousands of invertebrate species
Epiphytes like orchids and bromeliads rely entirely on canopy structure
Canopy studies require rope access, cranes, or walkway systems

faq.question: Why is the canopy called the last frontier of biodiversity?
faq.answer: The canopy is difficult to access and study. Scientists estimate that millions of canopy-dwelling species, particularly insects and fungi, remain undescribed. Each large tropical tree can host unique communities found nowhere else.

faq.question: What are epiphytes and why do they matter?
faq.answer: Epiphytes are plants that grow on other plants without parasitizing them, using the host for physical support. Orchids, ferns, mosses, and bromeliads create microhabitats and water traps that support frogs, insects, and birds high above the ground.
